A content delivery network is a system of computer servers spread across many cities that stores copies of websites so pages load quickly no matter where a visitor happens to be. Without this system, every request would travel to a single origin server, meaning the one original computer where a website's files actually live. That trip can be slow when the visitor is far away, like someone in Malaysia waiting on a server sitting in the United States. To fix this, copies of the site get placed on servers closer to visitors, called an edge location because it sits at the outer edge of the network, nearer everyday users than the origin ever could be. When a request arrives at that nearby location and the needed file is already stored there, this is called a cache hit, meaning the answer was ready on the spot with no long trip required. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of a popular book instead of everyone traveling to one faraway central archive. Fewer long trips means faster loading, less strain on the original server, and a smoother experience even during busy traffic spikes. Most modern websites, streaming platforms, and apps rely on this setup constantly, often invisibly, to feel instant.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It is the ultimate source everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a copy of the content | It shortens the distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | When requested content is found already stored nearby | It means near-instant delivery with no long trip |
| Latency | The delay caused by distance and network travel | Lower delay makes browsing feel fast and smooth |
